narrative:
The model predicts you have a 42% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. While students who passed had zero previous failures on average, your history of one failure strongly pushed the model toward expecting you to fail again. This single piece of information had the biggest influence on the outcome.

Two other factors worked in your favor but were not strong enough to overcome the past failure. Living in a smaller family (three or fewer members) is less common among students who passed—most successful students come from larger families—and this slightly increased the risk according to the model. Similarly, although you described your family relationships as good, this is actually a bit less positive than the average reported by students who passed, which also nudged the prediction slightly toward failure.

To improve, focus first on breaking the pattern of failing classes. Speak with your teachers about targeted help in the subjects that have been difficult, use the remedial courses offered, and try increasing your weekly study time beyond the two hours you currently spend. Small, consistent changes in these areas can meaningfully raise your chances of passing. (218 words)
